it-01.title: Why Do Countries Trade?
explain: **Trade** is the buying and selling of goods and services between countries. Selling to another country is called **exporting**, and buying from another country is called **importing**. International trade studies how these transactions come about and under what rules and prices they take place. All the countries, goods, and figures in this book are invented for the sake of explanation.

Making everything you use yourself is called **self-sufficiency**. But countries differ in climate, resources, technology, and the number of people available to work. One country has wide seas and catches fish well; another grows cotton on broad plains and makes cloth well. If each focuses on what it does well and they exchange the rest, they can consume more with the same effort. Concentrating on what one does well is called **specialization**, or the **division of labor**.

explain.alt: The left box, Sealand, says export fish, import cloth. The right box, Fieldland, says export cloth, import fish. Between the two boxes, an arrow carries fish to the right and an arrow carries cloth to the left.

explain:
The gains from trade are usually explained in three ways.
- **Variety**: you can use goods that are not produced at home.
- **Price**: buying from a place that produces more efficiently can lower prices.
- **Scale**: selling to many countries lets a producer make large quantities in one place, which can reduce the cost per unit.
However, the gains do not go equally to everyone. Domestic industries that compete with cheap imports can be hurt. This is why trade is always discussed in terms of both gains and burdens.

examples.title: An Analogy with Housework
body: In a household, if the person who cooks well does the cooking, the person who cleans well does the cleaning, and they share the results, both end up better off. Specialization and exchange between countries follow the same principle.
The difference is that within a country there may be particular groups that lose from this exchange.

it-02.title: Comparative Advantage and Opportunity Cost
explain: If a country can make everything better than others, does it have no need to trade? No. To understand why, we need **opportunity cost**. Opportunity cost is **the most valuable thing given up** in order to do something. If you spend a day catching fish, you cannot spend that time making cloth. That cloth is the opportunity cost of the fish.

If a country can produce more than another with the same resources, it is said to have an **absolute advantage**. If the opportunity cost of producing a good is lower than another country's, it has a **comparative advantage** in that good. What matters in trade is not absolute advantage but comparative advantage.

explain.alt: A table showing one worker's daily output. Sealand produces 12 tons of fish or 6 bolts of cloth; Fieldland produces 4 tons of fish or 4 bolts of cloth. The opportunity cost of 1 bolt of cloth is 2 tons of fish in Sealand and 1 ton of fish in Fieldland; the opportunity cost of 1 ton of fish is 0.5 bolt of cloth in Sealand and 1 bolt of cloth in Fieldland. The lower value in each pair is marked with a green border and bold text.

explain: In the table, Sealand produces more of both fish and cloth than Fieldland. But to make 1 bolt of cloth, Sealand gives up 2 tons of fish, while Fieldland gives up 1 ton. Opportunity cost is found by dividing the amount given up by the amount produced. For Sealand, 12 ÷ 6 = 2. So Fieldland has the comparative advantage in cloth, and Sealand has it in fish.
If the two countries concentrate on the goods in which they have a comparative advantage and exchange at a ratio between their two opportunity costs, both benefit.

examples.title: Exchanging 3 Bolts of Cloth
body: Suppose Fieldland exchanges 3 bolts of cloth for 4.5 tons of fish. That is 1.5 tons of fish per bolt of cloth. This ratio lies between the two countries' opportunity costs of 1 ton and 2 tons.
If Sealand made the 3 bolts of cloth itself, it would give up 6 tons of fish. By exchange it pays only 4.5 tons of fish, saving 1.5 tons.
If Fieldland had spent the effort used to make 3 bolts of cloth on catching fish instead, it would have gotten 3 tons of fish. By exchange it receives 4.5 tons, gaining 1.5 tons more. Both benefit.

it-03.title: Tariffs and Non-Tariff Barriers
explain: Countries sometimes increase imports and sometimes reduce them. Policies that block or hinder imports are called **trade barriers**. The most common is the **tariff**, a tax placed on imported goods. If the import price is $P$ and the tariff rate is $t$, the price with the tariff is as follows.

For example, if $P = 200$ won and $t = 0.15$, then $P' = 230$ won. When the price of an import rises, domestic producers of the same good are better off, the government collects tax, and consumers pay more.

explain.alt: Two bars. The left bar shows a price of 200 with no tariff; the right bar shows a price of 230 after the tariff is applied. A tariff of 30 is stacked in orange on top of the right bar.

explain:
There are also many barriers other than tariffs. These are called **non-tariff barriers**.
- **Import quota**: sets a limit on the quantity that may be brought in.
- **Technical regulations and standards**: set safety or environmental requirements and admit only goods that meet them.
- **Subsidy**: gives money to domestic producers to help them compete with imports.
Technical regulations often mix a legitimate purpose, such as protecting citizens' safety, with a purpose of keeping imports out, so it is not easy to tell the two apart.

Views on tariffs and barriers are divided. Those who support protection say that new industries that have not yet established themselves need time to grow, that industries related to security should be protected, and that jobs should be protected. Those who oppose it say that consumers end up paying higher prices, that other countries may impose retaliatory tariffs, and that protected industries may lose the incentive to improve efficiency. This book does not decide which side is right; it looks at both arguments together.

examples.title: Calculating a Tariff
body: If a 25% tariff is applied to a good with an import price of 400 won, the tariff is $400 \times 0.25 = 100$ won.
The price with the tariff is $400 + 100 = 500$ won. The same value is also obtained as $400 \times 1.25$.

it-04.title: Exchange Rates
explain: Because each country uses different money, trading requires converting one country's money into another's. The ratio at which two countries' currencies are exchanged is called the **exchange rate**. In this book Sealand uses the **wave** and Fieldland uses the **grain**, and we assume the exchange rate is 1 wave = 5 grains.
If an amount $A$ in waves is converted into grains, the amount in grains $B$ is as follows, where $r$ is the exchange rate.
$$B = A \times r$$
Conversely, to convert grains into waves, divide by $r$.

explain.alt: The left box shows 1 wave and the right box shows 5 grains. The arrow from left to right is labeled multiply by 5, and the arrow from right to left is labeled divide by 5. Below, a note says that if the wave rises in value, 1 wave buys more grains.

explain:
The exchange rate is not fixed; it changes. If 1 wave goes from 5 grains to 6 grains, the value of the wave has risen relative to the grain, and the value of the grain has fallen relatively. The direction of the effect on trade is as follows.
- For people in Sealand, Fieldland's goods become cheaper (favorable for imports).
- For people in Fieldland, Sealand's goods become more expensive (unfavorable for Sealand's exports).

If the value of the wave falls, the opposite happens. How much exports and imports actually change depends on the type of good, the time frame, and other conditions. Here we learn only the **direction** in which prices move.

If the wave rises to 1 wave = 6 grains, it is $60 \div 6 = 10$ waves. The same cloth has become cheaper for people in Sealand.

it-05.title: Trade Agreements and Rules
explain: Countries sometimes set rules for each other to follow when they trade. These are **trade agreements**. Some are made between two countries, and some among many countries. In reality, organizations such as the World Trade Organization (WTO) handle these rules, but here we learn only the basic concepts using imaginary countries.

The most common form is the **free trade agreement** (FTA). Countries that sign the agreement lower or eliminate tariffs among themselves, but each keeps its own tariffs on countries outside the agreement. By contrast, a **customs union** eliminates tariffs among its members and imposes a common tariff on outside countries.

explain.alt: The Sealand and Fieldland boxes are at the top, with a thick line between them labeled agreement 0%. Below, a Mountainland box is connected to each of the two countries by a thin line, and each line is labeled tariff 10%.

explain:
Agreements often include rules such as the following.
- **Most-favored-nation treatment**: the best terms given to one country are also given to other members.
- **National treatment**: once imports have entered, they are not treated differently from domestic goods.
- **Rules of origin**: the agreement's lower tariffs apply only to goods made in the agreement's member countries.

Rules of origin are needed because, if a country outside the agreement routes goods through a member country, it would get the lower tariff for free. Countries that do not receive the agreement's benefits can end up relatively disadvantaged, and when disputes arise, the parties try to settle them through the procedures the agreement sets out.

body: Suppose cloth made in Mountainland is sent to Fieldland, relabeled, and sold to Sealand. Should Sealand give it a 0% tariff? If rules of origin exist, this cloth is treated as a Mountainland good and charged 10%.
In this way, the rules ensure that the benefits of the agreement go only to member countries.

it-06.title: Reading Trade Data
explain: To read trade news, you need to know a few terms. The amount exported over a period is **export value**, and the amount imported is **import value**. The difference between them is the **trade balance**. If export value is $X$ and import value is $M$, it is as follows.
If $B$ is greater than 0 it is a **surplus**, if less than 0 a **deficit**, and if 0 the trade is balanced. The sum of export value and import value is used as a measure of a country's trade volume.

explain.alt: A grouped bar chart of imaginary Sealand's trade, in hundreds of millions of waves. Year 1: exports 80, imports 70, balance +10. Year 2: exports 90, imports 100, balance −10. Year 3: exports 110, imports 95, balance +15. Green is exports and orange is imports.

explain:
Points to keep in mind when reading data are as follows.
- First check the title, the **unit** (hundreds of millions of waves, etc.), and the period.
- When comparing two years, look not only at the difference but also at the **growth rate**. The growth rate is (later value − initial value) ÷ initial value, multiplied by 100.
- Do not assume that a deficit is automatically bad. If a country imports a lot of equipment that factories need, imports rise and a deficit can result.
- Check whether only trade in goods is counted or whether trade in services is included as well.
Numbers show only results; why those results came about must be asked separately.

Trade volume is $90 + 100 = 190$ hundred million waves. Exports grew from Year 1, but imports grew more, resulting in a deficit.

it-07.title: Comparative Advantage and the Terms of Trade
explain: In Stage 1 we saw that comparative advantage creates the gains from trade. But **at what ratio** must two countries exchange goods for both to gain? That ratio is the **terms of trade**. Where the terms of trade settle determines how the gains from trade are divided between the two countries.

The starting point of the Ricardian model is **opportunity cost**. Suppose that to make 1 semiconductor, Country A must give up 3 tons of rice, and Country B must give up 6 tons of rice (imaginary figures). Country A, where the opportunity cost of semiconductors is lower, has the comparative advantage in semiconductors, and Country B, where the opportunity cost of rice is lower (1 semiconductor = 6 tons of rice, so 1 ton of rice = 1/6 semiconductor), has it in rice. Which country is more efficient in absolute terms does not matter.

explain.alt: A number line with ticks from 0 to 8. The horizontal axis is "tons of rice exchanged for 1 semiconductor." At 3 it is marked "Country A domestic exchange ratio" and at 6 "Country B domestic exchange ratio," and the interval between 3 and 6 is shaded.

explain: Consider how many tons of rice should be exchanged for 1 semiconductor in trade. Country A can exchange 1 semiconductor for 3 tons of rice at home, so it has a reason to trade only if it receives **more than 3 tons**. Country B must give up 6 tons of rice at home to obtain 1 semiconductor, so it gains only if it pays **less than 6 tons**. Therefore the terms of trade that benefit both are **between the two countries' domestic exchange ratios**, that is, between 3 tons and 6 tons.

The closer the terms of trade are to one country's domestic exchange ratio, the more of the gains from trade the **other country** takes. If the terms of trade are 3.5 tons, Country B gains a lot (paying only 3.5 tons instead of 6) and Country A gains little (3.5 tons instead of 3). The actual terms of trade are determined by the relative size of the two countries' demand. In general, the terms of trade are measured as the export price index divided by the import price index, and when this value rises, the same exports can buy more imports.

Limitations: the Ricardian model treats labor as the only factor of production, assumes constant opportunity costs (a straight-line production possibility frontier), and assumes no transport costs. It therefore predicts complete specialization, but in reality a country often keeps several industries at once. That the gains from trade arise for the country as a whole but do not go evenly to **everyone within the country** is covered in the next lesson. This lesson uses only imaginary countries and figures.

body: Conditions (imaginary): the two countries in the figure, with terms of trade of 1 semiconductor = 4.5 tons of rice.
Step 1: If Country A exports 10 semiconductors, it receives 45 tons of rice. Exchanging 10 semiconductors for rice at home would give 30 tons, so the gain is 15 tons.
Step 2: Country B obtains 10 semiconductors for 45 tons of rice. Making them itself would require giving up 60 tons of rice, so its gain is 15 tons. Both countries gain.

Step 2: Even when it exports the same quantity, the quantity it can import has fallen by about 14%. The terms of trade have deteriorated.

it-08.title: The Heckscher-Ohlin Model and the Income Distribution Effects of Trade
explain: The Ricardian model held that trade arises because technology differs from country to country. But trade is also lively between countries with similar technology. Heckscher and Ohlin offered a different cause: **countries have different amounts of the factors of production (labor, capital, land)**.

**The Heckscher-Ohlin theorem**: each country has a comparative advantage in, and exports, the good that **intensively uses the factor it has in relative abundance**. A labor-abundant country exports labor-intensive goods (garment assembly), and a capital-abundant country exports capital-intensive goods (precision machinery). The abundant factor is relatively cheap, so goods that use a lot of that factor can also be made cheaply.

A powerful consequence of this model is **income distribution**. **The Stolper-Samuelson theorem**: when the relative price of a good rises, the real income of the factor used intensively in that good rises, and the real income of the other factor falls. When a capital-abundant country begins to trade, the price of the capital-intensive good (the export) rises, so **owners of capital can gain**, while **workers can lose** if they compete with the labor-intensive good (the import). Even if the country as a whole gains, **there are winners and losers**.

**The factor price equalization theorem**: if trade equalizes the prices of goods, then under certain conditions the factor prices (wages, rate of return on capital) of the two countries also move closer to each other. This is because buying and selling goods is, indirectly, like buying and selling factors. In reality, differences in technology, transport costs, and trade barriers keep them from becoming fully equal.

Evidence and limitations: the **Leontief paradox** is the finding that the exports of a country thought to be capital-abundant turned out to be labor-intensive; it showed that the quality (skill) of labor and technological differences must also be considered. Also, **intra-industry trade**, in which similar countries exchange products of the same industry (exporting cars while also importing them), is explained by economies of scale and product differentiation, which lie outside the Heckscher-Ohlin model. This is where policy discussions about retraining and job-transition support for the losers from trade come from. This lesson uses only imaginary cases.

it-09.title: The Welfare Effects of Tariffs
explain: A tariff is a tax placed on imports. When a tariff is imposed, domestic producers are protected and the government collects tax. But consumers pay a higher price. Who gains and loses how much, and what happens to the country as a whole, is analyzed using **consumer surplus** and **producer surplus**.

**Consumer surplus** is the sum of the differences between what consumers were willing to pay and the price they actually paid (the area below the demand curve and above the price). **Producer surplus** is the sum of the differences between the price producers received and the minimum amount they needed to receive (the supply curve), which is the area below the price and above the supply curve. The sum of the two surpluses and government revenue is the welfare of society as a whole.

explain.alt: A supply and demand diagram for the importing country's market. The horizontal axis is quantity (0 to 100) and the vertical axis is price (0 to 100). The supply line starts from the origin and the demand line starts from a price of 100. Horizontal dotted lines mark the world price of 20 and the post-tariff price of 30. Between the two dotted lines, from left to right, are region a (from the price axis to the supply line), b (a small triangle next to the supply line, quantity 20 to 30), c (a rectangle between quantities 30 and 70), and d (a small triangle next to the demand line, quantity 70 to 80).

explain: When a small country (one that cannot affect the world price) imposes a tariff, the domestic price rises to the world price plus the tariff. In the figure, when the price rises from 20 to 30: domestic production rises from 20 to 30, consumption falls from 80 to 70, and imports fall from 60 to 40. **Producer surplus** rises by a, **government tariff revenue** is c (tariff × quantity imported), and **consumer surplus** falls by a + b + c + d.

The net effect is $-(b + d)$. **b is the production distortion loss**: goods that could be bought in the world market at 20 are made at home at a higher cost (between 20 and 30), wasting resources. **d is the consumption distortion loss**: consumers who would have bought at the world price give up consumption because of the higher price. The two triangles together are called the **deadweight loss**. For a small country, a tariff reduces the welfare of the country as a whole.

Exceptions and limitations: a **large country** can use a tariff to reduce import demand and lower the world price (the terms-of-trade effect), and if that gain is larger than the deadweight loss, welfare may rise. However, if the partner country retaliates, both lose. The **infant industry argument** holds that an industry that is not yet competitive but will grow in future should be temporarily protected, but there are many cases where the protected industry never becomes self-sufficient. An import quota has a price effect similar to a tariff, but the gain corresponding to c goes not to the government but to those who hold import licenses.

it-10.title: The Balance of Payments and Exchange Rate Determination
explain: The record of all economic transactions a country carries out with foreign countries is the **balance of payments**. It includes exports and imports, overseas investment, and even interest and dividends. The balance of payments creates demand and supply in the foreign exchange market and moves the **exchange rate**.

The balance of payments is broadly divided into two parts. The **current account**: the goods balance (exports − imports), the services balance (transport, travel, intellectual property royalties), the primary income balance (interest and dividends on overseas investment, income from work abroad), and the secondary income balance (grants, remittances). The **financial account**: changes in direct investment, portfolio investment, other investment, and reserve assets. Because it is recorded by double-entry bookkeeping, apart from errors and omissions, **the current account = the net increase in assets in the financial account**. A country with a current account surplus accumulates foreign assets by that amount.

The **exchange rate** is the ratio at which two currencies are exchanged. If the won/dollar exchange rate rises from 1,200 won to 1,300 won, more won are needed to buy 1 dollar, so the won has **depreciated**. It is easy to be confused that a rising number means a fall in the value of one's own currency.

In the foreign exchange market, **demand** for dollars comes from payments for imports and from overseas investment, and **supply** comes from export revenue and foreign investment in the home country. If imports rise or foreign capital leaves, dollar demand rises and the won/dollar exchange rate goes up. Conversely, if exports rise or foreign investment flows in, the exchange rate falls. When the exchange rate rises, the foreign-currency price of exports becomes cheaper, so exports tend to rise and imports to fall, improving the current account.

Exchange rate changes affect the trade balance with a **time lag**. When the won depreciates, at first the amount of won needed to pay for already contracted imports is higher, so the current account may in fact worsen before improving as export and import volumes adjust over time; this is the **J-curve effect**. Limitation: short-term exchange rates are heavily swayed by interest rates, expectations, and risk aversion, and cannot be explained by trade flows alone. The valuation theories in the next lesson address this. This lesson is conceptual and is not foreign exchange trading or investment advice.

it-11.title: Purchasing Power Parity and Interest Rate Parity
explain: What determines exchange rates in the long run, and in the short run? International finance uses two parity conditions as reference points: **purchasing power parity** (PPP) in the long run and **interest rate parity** (IRP) for short-term capital movements. Both rest on the arbitrage logic that "the same thing should have the same price."

**The law of one price**: without transport costs and trade barriers, the same good should have the same price in every country. Otherwise there would be arbitrage, buying where it is cheap and selling where it is dear. **Absolute PPP**, which extends this to price levels as a whole, is $S = P/P^*$ (exchange rate = domestic price level / foreign price level). **Relative PPP** is written in terms of rates of change. $$\text{환율 변화율} \approx \pi - \pi^*$$ (the left side is the rate of change of the exchange rate, 환율 변화율). If domestic inflation is 3 percentage points higher than abroad, the home currency depreciates by about 3% per year.

PPP does not fit well in the short run. This is because of non-traded goods (haircuts, rent), transport costs, tariffs, and price stickiness. However, it explains the **long-run direction** and the exchange rate trends of high-inflation countries well. Indexes that compare the prices of the same product across countries are used to compare the PPP exchange rate with the actual exchange rate and gauge whether a currency is overvalued or undervalued.

**Interest rate parity**: if capital moves freely, the returns on domestic and foreign deposits, once exchange rate changes are taken into account, should be equal. **Covered interest rate parity** (CIP) is the case in which currency risk is eliminated with a forward contract. $$\frac{F}{S} = \frac{1 + i}{1 + i^*}$$ $F$는 선물환율, $S$는 현물환율, $i$와 $i^*$는 국내·외국 금리다. (That is, F is the forward exchange rate, S is the spot exchange rate, and i and i* are the domestic and foreign interest rates.) If the domestic interest rate is higher, the forward rate is higher than the spot rate (the home currency trades at a forward discount). The gain from the higher interest rate is offset by the forward discount.

**Uncovered interest rate parity** (UIP) uses the expected future exchange rate instead of the forward rate. It means that the currency of the country with the higher interest rate is expected to depreciate by that same amount in the future. Empirically, UIP often fails, and there are many cases where a currency with a high interest rate actually appreciates (a risk premium). This lesson is theory and is not foreign exchange trading advice.

it-12.title: Currency Risk and Hedging Strategies
explain: The won value of the 1 million dollars an exporter will receive in three months can differ by tens of millions of won depending on the exchange rate in the meantime. However much profit the core business earns, exchange rate movements can cause losses. This risk is **currency risk** (or exchange rate risk), and it is a management task that firms engaged in international transactions cannot avoid.

Three types of currency risk: (1) **Transaction risk**: the change in value of a foreign currency transaction that has been contracted but not yet settled (the most direct). (2) **Translation risk**: the accounting change that arises when an overseas subsidiary's financial statements are converted into the home currency. (3) **Economic risk**: the risk that exchange rate changes alter a firm's competitiveness and future cash flows over the long run (for example, a long-term appreciation of the home currency weakens export competitiveness).

**External hedging instruments**: (1) **Forward contract**: you agree now to buy or sell foreign currency at a fixed rate on a specific future date. It fixes the result completely but also gives up the gains from favorable movements. (2) **Currency option**: you pay a premium and protect only against the unfavorable direction (buying a dollar put option limits the loss if the exchange rate falls while keeping the gain if it rises). (3) **Currency swap**: principal and interest in different currencies are exchanged over the long term.

**Internal hedging methods**: first consider methods that cost nothing. **Matching**: match dollar receipts with dollar payments (if raw materials are bought in dollars, they offset the dollar export revenue). **Leading and lagging**: bring forward or delay the timing of settlement according to the exchange rate outlook. **Choice of invoicing currency**: contract in the home currency to pass the risk to the counterparty (when you have bargaining power). **Netting**: offset receivables and payables between companies in the same group to reduce the amount actually exchanged.

The purpose of hedging is not profit but **reducing uncertainty**. It is not necessary to hedge every risk. The **hedge ratio** is set by comparing the cost of hedging (option premium, the opportunity cost of a forward contract), the size of the risk, and the range of fluctuation the company can bear. Limitation: if an expected transaction whose volume or timing is uncertain is over-hedged, then when the transaction does not materialize, the hedge contract itself becomes a speculative position. This lesson is conceptual and is not advice on actual foreign exchange trading.

it-13.title: Basic Principles of the WTO Multilateral Trading System
explain: If each country raised tariffs and blocked imports as it pleased, retaliation would follow retaliation and everyone would lose. The protectionist race of the Great Depression in the 1930s is an example. After the Second World War, countries decided to make trade rules together, and the result was the GATT and the **World Trade Organization (WTO)** that succeeded it. The WTO system rests on a few simple principles.

**Most-favored-nation (MFN) treatment**: any trade advantage (such as a lower tariff) given to one country must be given equally to all other members. It is the principle of not discriminating against particular countries. Thanks to this, large and small countries enjoy the same terms, and a single tariff cut spreads to all members.

**National treatment (NT)**: once imports have crossed the border and entered the domestic market, they must be treated the same as domestic goods. A country must not impose a higher consumption tax on the same product than on the domestic product, or apply stricter sales regulations. If MFN treatment prohibits discrimination **among foreign countries**, national treatment prohibits discrimination **between foreign and domestic goods**.

Other principles: **bindings and transparency** (not exceeding committed tariff ceilings, and making trade regulations public), **prohibition of quantitative restrictions** (using price instruments such as tariffs instead of quotas), and **dispute settlement procedures** (resolving disputes through panels and appeals rather than unilateral retaliation). WTO decisions are, in principle, made by the **consensus** of the members.

There are also **exceptions**. Free trade agreements (FTAs) and customs unions are allowed as exceptions to MFN treatment if they meet certain conditions (such as liberalizing substantially all trade). There are also preferential treatment for developing countries, measures to protect public health and the environment (which must not be discriminatory or a disguised restriction on trade), national security exceptions, and the trade remedy measures of the next lesson. Limitations: with so many members, new multilateral agreements are very hard to reach, and there have been periods when dispute settlement did not function smoothly. This lesson is conceptual and is not actual legal advice on trade law.

it-14.title: Trade Remedies: Anti-Dumping, Countervailing Duties, and Safeguards
explain: Even under the principle of free trade, there are cases where imports cause serious harm to a domestic industry. In such situations the WTO allows **trade remedy** measures, such as imposing additional tariffs, if certain procedures and requirements are met. There are three, of which the first two respond to **unfair** trade, and the last responds to a surge in imports even when trade is **fair**.

**Anti-dumping duties**: when a foreign firm exports a product at a price lower than its selling price in its home market (the normal value), this is called **dumping**. If dumping causes material injury to the importing country's industry and the causal link is proved, an anti-dumping duty can be imposed within the range of the **dumping margin** (normal value − export price). The dumping margin rate is often calculated as follows (정상가격 = normal value, 수출가격 = export price): dumping margin rate $= \frac{\text{정상가격} - \text{수출가격}}{\text{수출가격}}$.

**Countervailing duties**: when the exporting country's government gives an exporting firm a specific subsidy (an export subsidy, support for a particular industry), artificially raising its price competitiveness, and the importing country's industry is injured as a result, a duty **equal to the size of the subsidy** is imposed to offset it. If anti-dumping targets the conduct of firms, countervailing duties target the subsidies of governments.

**Safeguards (emergency import restrictions)**: even without unfair practices, if imports of a particular product **surge** and cause **serious injury** to a domestic industry, a country can temporarily raise tariffs or restrict imports. Because the trade is not unfair, the requirements are stricter, the measure is in principle applied to all exporting countries without discrimination, it is limited in duration, and compensation may have to be given to the affected exporting countries. The purpose is to give the domestic industry time to restructure.

Limitations and debate: the result of an anti-dumping measure varies greatly depending on how the "normal value" is calculated, and there is criticism that in practice it is abused as a tool of protectionism. Trade remedies impose costs on consumers in the importing country and on downstream industries that use imported inputs. This lesson is conceptual and is not legal advice on filing or responding to an actual trade remedy case.

it-15.title: FTAs and Rules of Origin
explain: When an FTA is signed, tariffs on member countries' goods are lowered or eliminated. But what counts as a "member country's good"? If goods from a non-member country merely pass through an FTA member and receive duty-free treatment, the FTA loses its meaning. **Rules of origin** prevent this. Whether an FTA is used successfully depends largely on whether the rules of origin are met.

Criteria for determining origin: (1) **Wholly obtained criterion**: goods wholly obtained or produced in one country (crops grown in that country, minerals mined there). (2) **Substantial transformation criterion**: for goods made using materials from several countries, the country where the last "substantial transformation" took place is regarded as the country of origin. There are three ways to judge substantial transformation.

**Change in tariff classification**: if the customs classification number (HS code) of the materials and the finished good differs by a certain level or more, it is regarded as substantial transformation. For example, making furniture (Chapter 94) from logs (Chapter 44) changes the chapter. **Regional value content**: the value added within the region must be at least a certain percentage. The commonly used build-down method is as follows (역내 부가가치 비율 = regional value content, 상품 가격 = price of the good, 역외산 재료비 = cost of non-originating materials): $$\text{역내 부가가치 비율} = \frac{\text{상품 가격} - \text{역외산 재료비}}{\text{상품 가격}} \times 100$$ **Specific processing requirement**: a specific process (for example, dyeing and cutting of fabric) must be carried out within the region.

Concepts that matter in practice: **cumulation** (recognizing materials from other FTA member countries as if they were domestic), **de minimis** (ignoring non-originating materials if they make up a very small percentage), **direct consignment** (originating goods must not be processed while passing through a third country), and **proof of origin** (a certificate issued or self-certification, with an obligation to keep supporting documents). Incorrectly declaring origin can lead to revocation of the preference and recovery of unpaid duties.

Limitations and issues: because different FTAs have different rules of origin, companies face the complexity of complying with each (the **spaghetti bowl effect**). If the cost of managing origin exceeds the tariff benefit, firms do not use the FTA. This lesson treats the concepts with imaginary countries and figures and is not advice on actual origin determination or customs clearance.

Step 1: Regional value content $= (200 - 120)/200 = 40\%$.
Step 2: It meets the standard exactly. Even a small rise in the price of non-originating parts would miss the standard. Switching some non-originating parts to originating ones creates a margin.

it-16.title: Incoterms 2020: The Transfer of Risk and Cost
explain: In an international transaction, goods leave the factory and travel by truck, port, ship, and again port and truck before reaching the buyer. If an accident happens along the way, who is responsible? Who pays the freight and insurance? So that these need not be negotiated at length each time, the International Chamber of Commerce created standard rules. These are the **Incoterms**, and the version in wide use today is the 2020 revision.

Using three-letter abbreviations, Incoterms set **the point at which risk transfers**, **the extent of cost allocation**, and **the division of obligations** such as export and import customs clearance. An important caution: Incoterms **do not determine when ownership transfers or the terms of payment**. These are set separately by the sales contract and the payment terms.

explain.alt: The route of the goods runs from left to right: the seller's factory, loading at the port of export, arrival at the port of import, and the buyer's named place. Below it, orange lines for five terms show the seller's risk span. EXW ends at the seller's factory, FOB and CIF end at loading at the port of export, and DAP and DDP extend to the buyer's named place.

explain: Representative terms: **EXW** (Ex Works): the seller is done once the goods are handed over at its own factory, and the buyer bears almost all risk and cost. **FOB** (Free On Board, sea transport only): risk passes to the buyer **at the moment the goods are loaded on the ship** at the port of export. The buyer pays the sea freight. **CIF** (Cost, Insurance and Freight, sea transport only): the seller pays freight to the port of destination and the premium for minimum insurance cover, but **risk transfers at loading, exactly as under FOB**. The key point of the C-term group is that the point where costs divide and the point where risk divides are different. **DAP** (Delivered at Place): the seller bears the risk and cost up to the destination and hands over the goods ready for unloading. **DDP** (Delivered Duty Paid): in addition to DAP, the seller bears **import clearance and even the import duties**.

Principles for choosing a term: for cargo such as containers that is handed to a carrier inland before reaching the port, it is recommended that the terms for delivery to a carrier (FCA, CIP) are more suitable than FOB and CIF. A seller who is unfamiliar with the other country's customs procedures and uses DDP may bear unexpected taxes and procedural burdens, and conversely, under EXW the seller has no obligation for export clearance, so the buyer bears the burden of handling clearance in a foreign country. This lesson is conceptual and is not advice on drafting an actual contract.

it-17.title: The Structure of Letter of Credit Settlement
explain: When trading with a distant partner for the first time, the exporter worries, "What if I ship the goods and am not paid?" and the importer worries, "What if I send the money and the goods never arrive?" The device that solves this problem of mutual distrust through the credit of a bank is the **letter of credit** (L/C).

A letter of credit is a document in which the importer's bank (the **issuing bank**) promises the exporter (the **beneficiary**), "If you present documents that conform to the terms written in the letter of credit, we will pay." The exporter can ship relying not on the importer but on the **bank's promise to pay**, and the importer gains the assurance that payment goes out only if conforming documents (such as a bill of lading, evidence that the goods were shipped) are presented.

explain.alt: A flow diagram of a letter of credit transaction. Top left, the importer (applicant); top right, the exporter (beneficiary); bottom left, the issuing bank (importing country); bottom right, the advising bank (exporting country). (1) importer → issuing bank: application to open; (2) issuing bank → advising bank: issuance of the letter of credit; (3) advising bank → exporter: advice; (4) exporter → importer: shipment of goods. Below it says "Afterward (5) presentation of documents → (6) payment after examination of documents."

explain: The flow: (1) The importer applies to the issuing bank to open a letter of credit. (2) The issuing bank issues the letter of credit and sends it to the **advising bank** in the exporting country. (3) The advising bank checks its authenticity and advises the exporter. (4) The exporter ships the goods and assembles documents such as the bill of lading, commercial invoice, and insurance policy. (5) The exporter presents the documents to the bank. (6) The bank examines **only whether the documents conform** to the terms of the letter of credit, and pays. The importer reimburses the bank, receives the documents, and uses the bill of lading to take delivery of the goods.

Two principles of the letter of credit: **Independence**: the letter of credit is a transaction separate from the sales contract. Even if there is a dispute under the sales contract, the bank considers only the terms of the letter of credit. **Abstraction (a transaction in documents)**: the bank looks only at the **documents**, not the goods. If the documents conform to the terms, it pays even if there is a problem with the actual goods, and if the documents have a minor discrepancy, it may refuse to pay even if the goods are perfect. So the exporter must match the documents strictly.

Limitations: a letter of credit involves fees and cumbersome paperwork, and payment is often refused because of document discrepancies. Since the bank looks only at documents, the importer reduces quality risk by putting documents such as a pre-shipment inspection certificate into the terms. Once the parties come to know each other well, they move to simpler methods such as remittance or collection. This lesson is conceptual and is not advice on actual letter of credit work.

it-18.title: International Transport and Marine Insurance
explain: Most traded goods cross the sea. The mode of transport, the transport documents, and the insurance against accidents together with the Incoterms and letters of credit above form the backbone of international transactions. This lesson covers the nature of transport documents and the basic principles of marine insurance.

**Sea transport** is divided into **liner shipping** (container ships), which run on fixed routes and schedules, and **tramp shipping** (bulk cargo such as crude oil and grain), in which a whole ship is chartered at the shipper's request. Containers, with their standardized sizes (20-foot and 40-foot), made transshipment between ships, trains, and trucks fast and greatly lowered trade costs. **Multimodal transport**, in which one carrier takes responsibility across ship, rail, and road, is also common.

The **bill of lading** (B/L) is evidence that the carrier has received or loaded the cargo, **evidence of the contract of carriage**, and most importantly, **a document of title to the goods**. The original bill of lading must be presented at the destination to take delivery of the cargo, and when the bill of lading is transferred (by endorsement and delivery), the rights to the cargo are transferred as well. This is why, in letter of credit transactions, a bank can hold the bill of lading as security. By contrast, an **air waybill** is not a document of title but only evidence of the contract of carriage, so the person named as consignee receives the cargo.

**Marine insurance** compensates for damage to cargo caused by accidents in transit. Forms of loss: **total loss**, in which the whole cargo is lost, and **partial loss**, in which only part is damaged. In particular, **general average** is a system in which, when a sacrifice has been made, such as deliberately jettisoning some cargo to save the ship and the whole cargo, the loss is shared among the ship and all cargo interests in proportion to value. Insurance terms range from basic to broad according to the scope of cover, and the broader the cover, the higher the premium. Under CIF and CIP terms the seller takes out the insurance, but the insurable interest lies with the buyer who bears the risk.

Principles of insurance: **insurable interest** (one must have an interest that can suffer loss), **utmost good faith** (important facts must not be concealed), and **indemnity** (one is not compensated for more than the actual loss). The insured amount is commonly set at 110% of the commercial invoice amount, the extra 10% being a practice that reflects expected profit. This lesson is conceptual and is not advice on actual transport or insurance contracts.

Step 1: Total contributory value $= 600 + 100 + 200 + 100 = 1000$; the loss is 100, so the contribution rate is 10%.
Step 2: The shipowner bears 60, A bears 10, B bears 20, and C bears 10. A lost 100 but bears only 10, so the remaining 90 is compensated by the other parties.

it-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Total Cost and Risk Design for a Hypothetical Import Transaction
explain: The first capstone lesson designs one hypothetical import transaction from start to finish using the tools of Stages 2 to 5. Tariffs (origin), exchange rates (hedging), Incoterms (risk and cost), and payment (letters of credit) are intertwined in a single transaction. All countries and figures are imaginary.

**Situation**: a furniture company in Country Gap chooses between log suppliers in Country Eul (an FTA partner) and Country Byeong (no FTA). The log price is 108,000 dollars FOB Eul and 100,000 dollars FOB Byeong. Sea freight and insurance are about 6,000 dollars from both. Gap's tariff on logs is 8% in general and 0% for Eul-origin goods under the FTA preference (proof of origin required). Payment is in dollars in three months; the current exchange rate is 1,200 won and the three-month forward rate is 1,210 won.

**Step 1 (tariff)**: tariffs are usually applied to the customs value including freight and insurance (CIF basis). Byeong: customs value $106{,}000$ dollars × 8% = 8,480 dollars, for a total of 114,480 dollars. Eul: customs value 114,000 dollars, tariff 0, total 114,000 dollars. The FOB price is cheaper from Byeong, but once the tariff is included, **Eul is 480 dollars better**. However, the Eul-origin goods must meet the rules of origin and the proof must be in order.

**Step 2 (exchange rate)**: the total of 114,000 dollars for the Eul transaction is paid in three months. If it is not hedged and the exchange rate becomes 1,300 won, the won burden rises by about 11.4 million won. If the dollars are bought forward at 1,210 won, the cost is fixed at $114{,}000 \times 1{,}210 \approx 1$ eok (100 million) plus 37.94 million, that is, about 137.94 million won.

**Step 3 (Incoterms, insurance, payment)**: if buying FOB, the Gap company bears the risk of sea transport and must take out marine insurance itself (the practice is to insure at 110% of the CIF amount). Because this is a first transaction with the supplier, a letter of credit is used, and the certificate of origin and a pre-shipment inspection certificate are put into the required documents, managing the FTA preference and quality risk together.

**Critique**: Eul's advantage (480 dollars) is small enough to be reversed easily by a difference in freight or by a failure of proof of origin. The cost of managing proof of origin, the letter of credit fees, and supply stability (single-source risk) must also be weighed. Spreading risk (using both suppliers in parallel) may be worth more than a small difference in total cost.

it-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: A Global Supply Chain Trade Design Report
explain: The final task is to **design one hypothetical international transaction (an export or an import), write a report integrating tariffs, origin, currency risk, Incoterms, payment, and insurance, and critique that design**. It uses only imaginary countries and figures, and is not material for actual trade policy, legal, or investment decisions.

Report framework: (1) **Transaction overview**: the product, the exporting and importing countries, quantity, and price (imaginary). (2) **Basis for trade**: why buy and sell between these countries (comparative advantage, factor endowments, product differentiation). (3) **Trade rules**: the applicable tariff, whether the FTA and its origin criteria are met, and the possibility of trade remedy measures. (4) **Terms of the transaction**: the choice of Incoterm and the reason, the mode of transport, and insurance. (5) **Payment and finance**: the payment method (letter of credit, remittance, etc.), currency risk exposure, and hedging. (6) **Summary of total cost and risk**: the landed cost, the main risks, and the responses. (7) **Critique**: how the design is shaken if assumptions change (a tariff increase, a sudden exchange rate move, a failure of origin, the triggering of a trade remedy).

Features of a good design: the elements are **consistent with one another** (you do not buy FOB and forget insurance; you put proof of origin in the documents required under the letter of credit). Costs are compared on a **landed cost** basis. Risk is not eliminated; it is made clear **who bears how much of it**. Figures are given with their basis, and sensitive assumptions are shown as scenarios.
This task is not scored. What you submit is saved only on this device and can be viewed again under 'What I left' in 'My progress'.
